opus-5.5.text:
I think small teams still have a lot of room, but you have to be honest about where that room is.

If the game is purely about pre-training the biggest frontier model, small teams aren't really in the competition. That race is about capital, compute, data pipelines, and very large engineering organizations. A team of ten or twenty people isn't going to out-scale a company spending billions on GPUs, and pretending otherwise isn't helpful.

But AI innovation has never been only about the biggest model. Looking back at how deep learning developed, many of the important ideas came from small groups. AlexNet was essentially a couple of people with a few GPUs. A lot of the framework work, including Caffe, which I started as a grad student, came from very small teams solving a problem they personally felt. Small teams tend to see the pain points earlier because they're closer to the actual usage.

Today I see a few areas where small teams have real advantages.

The first is efficiency. When compute is expensive and scarce, there's a lot of value in making models cheaper to train, faster to serve, and easier to deploy. Inference optimization, distillation, quantization, better systems software, better scheduling of GPU resources: much of this is engineering craftsmanship rather than raw scale. A focused team can make a big difference there.

The second is the application and vertical layer. Foundation models are becoming something like infrastructure. The question then becomes who understands a specific workflow, a specific customer, or a specific dataset well enough to build something people will pay for. Big companies can't cover every vertical deeply, so small teams can move faster and iterate with real users.

The third is the open-source ecosystem. Open models have changed the landscape. A small team no longer has to start from zero. It can take a strong open base model, fine-tune it, build tooling around it, and compete on product and speed rather than on pre-training budget.

The caution I'd add is that small teams need to pick problems that won't be wiped out by the next release from a large model company. If your entire value is a thin wrapper around someone else's API, that's fragile. You want to build something where the model getting better makes your product better, not obsolete.

So overall I'm optimistic. The center of gravity at the very top is concentrated, but the surface area of AI keeps expanding, and most of that surface area will be explored by small teams.

r001.rationale: The response describes the frontier-model race as depending on capital, compute, data pipelines, and engineering organizations, but does not characterize it as a competition for talent.

r002.rationale: It says important AI ideas came from small groups and gives AlexNet and Caffe as examples of work from very small teams.

r003.rationale: The response discusses how open models help small teams build products, but does not say internet companies pursue open source to attract talent.

r004.rationale: It says large companies cannot cover every vertical deeply, but does not explain how commitments to existing businesses’ resource allocation hinder innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Let me answer this honestly, because I think there's a lot of hype on both sides of this question.

I'll separate it into two layers. If we're talking about training the very largest foundation models from scratch, the frontier models, I think small teams should be realistic. That game is about compute, data, and the ability to keep burning money for a long time before you see returns. A team of ten people with a few million dollars simply isn't going to out-train an organization with tens of thousands of GPUs. That's not a comment on talent. Some of the best researchers I know are in small teams. It's just that at the frontier, capital and infrastructure are the gating factors, and the gap compounds.

But I'd argue that's a very narrow definition of innovation, and it's not where most of the value will be created. When I was working on Caffe at Berkeley, we were a tiny group. We didn't have the biggest models or the most data. What we had was a clear idea about what practitioners actually needed, which was a framework that was fast, readable, and easy to deploy. That turned out to matter a lot. The same thing happened over and over in the history of this field: the big breakthroughs in infrastructure, tooling, and system efficiency often came from small groups who understood a specific pain point deeply.

So for small teams today, I'd point to three areas where I think they can genuinely win.

The first is the layer between models and applications. Serving, inference optimization, cost reduction, latency. The foundation models are increasingly commoditized, and the open-source ecosystem is strong enough that you don't need to own the base model to build something valuable on top of it. If you can make the same model run three times cheaper or faster, that's real engineering leverage, and large organizations are often too slow or too internally focused to do it well.

The second is domain depth. Big labs build general models. They don't have the time or the incentive to understand what a logistics company or a hospital or a semiconductor fab actually needs. A small team that combines solid ML engineering with real domain understanding can build something that's much more useful than a general model, and the incumbents won't catch up easily because the hard part isn't the model, it's the knowledge.

The third is speed. A small team can decide something on Monday and ship it on Wednesday. In a field that's moving this fast, that's an enormous advantage. The large organizations have their own gravity: alignment meetings, roadmap reviews, political considerations. Small teams can ride on top of every new open-source release the week it comes out.

The thing I'd caution against is small teams trying to mimic the big players. If your pitch is "we're going to train a slightly smaller version of what the big labs already have," that's a hard place to be. You'll always be a year behind and short on money. The better question is: what can we do that they structurally can't or won't?

So my overall assessment is actually optimistic. The frontier model race is a game for a handful of companies. But the ecosystem around those models, the infrastructure, the applications, the tools that make this technology usable, that's a much bigger space, and it looks a lot like the early days of cloud or the early days of deep learning frameworks. Small, focused teams with strong engineering did very well in those eras. I think they'll do well in this one too, as long as they're clear-eyed about which game they're playing.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier competition is gated by compute, data, capital, and infrastructure, and explicitly says that is not a comment on talent.

r002.rationale: It describes small teams as sources of major advances in infrastructure, tooling, and efficiency, citing Caffe and saying focused teams can win in several areas.

r003.rationale: It mentions the open-source ecosystem as an opportunity for small teams, but does not say internet companies pursue open source to attract talent.

r004.rationale: It says large organizations can be slow because of meetings, reviews, and politics, but does not connect this to commitments to allocating resources across existing businesses.

astra-6.text:
I think small teams still have a lot of room to innovate. But we should distinguish technical innovation from competing on sheer scale. If the goal is to train a larger model using the same approach as everyone else, that requires a lot of capital, computing resources, and infrastructure. A small team will have a hard time winning on those terms.

The opportunity is to find something that the current approach doesn’t do well. Can you make training more efficient? Can you reduce the cost of inference? Can you get better results for a particular task with a smaller model and better data? Those are technical problems where a good idea can matter more than the size of the team.

Small teams also have the advantage of focus. They can pick a problem, test an idea, and change direction quickly. Of course, being small doesn’t automatically make you innovative—you still need a strong technical insight and a way to validate it.

So I wouldn’t judge their prospects only by whether they can build the biggest foundation model. I’d look at whether they can identify an important bottleneck and solve it substantially better. There’s still plenty of space for that.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts innovation with competing on model scale, but does not characterize the competition as a competition for talent.

r002.rationale: It says small teams have substantial room to innovate and can solve important technical bottlenecks substantially better, including through efficiency, inference cost, or task-specific models.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention internet companies or open source as a way to attract talent.

r004.rationale: The response says large-scale model training requires resources, but does not discuss large companies’ existing businesses or how their resource commitments hinder innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think small teams still have a lot of room to innovate, but it helps to distinguish between training a general-purpose model from scratch and making a meaningful technical contribution. If you’re competing purely on model size, the demands for compute, data, and capital put a small team at a disadvantage.

But technical progress isn’t just about scale. A small team can focus on a specific problem—making inference more efficient, improving how a model uses domain knowledge, or building a better way to evaluate its performance. A focused team can move quickly, test an idea, and learn from users without coordinating across a large organization.

So I wouldn’t frame it as, ‘Can a small team beat a large company at everything?’ The question is where that team has an insight and can turn it into a measurable improvement. Large companies have resources; small teams can have focus. There’s room for both.
